item.title: Venture-backed startups use AI and FOIA requests to map government spending data
item.description:
Venture-backed startups use AI and FOIA requests to map government spending data

Venture-backed startups have raised over $100 million to collect data from thousands of government agencies, using AI to turn that information into “signals” that help businesses sell to governments. This trend has altered the landscape of public records requests, shifting from annual volume to high-frequency, specific data collection.

📜 The Shift in FOIA Requests

The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, with every state now having its own version in law. Historically, commercial requesters have dominated this system. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University, documented this trend in her 2016 study “FOIA, Inc.,” finding that commercial requesters accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration.

In Panton, Vermont, town clerk Kyle Rowe observed this change firsthand. Panton used to receive a request every year or so from SmartProcure for “all purchasing records.” Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Subsequently, different companies began making more specific requests, such as records for every purchase related to emergency road flares. In Chautauqua County, New York, a local paralegal was hired this summer after seeing requests double, an increase the county attorney blamed on automated activity.

🏢 Key Players and Funding

Several companies have built their businesses around this model, raising significant capital to scale their operations:

  • SmartProcure (GovSpend): Pioneered the model 15 years ago with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. The company sends roughly 180,000 requests per year.
  • Starbridge: Has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures, to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data.”
  • Pursuit: Backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, it has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers using an “industrial-scale FOIA operation.” It also sends roughly 180,000 requests per year.
  • PinPoint Analytics: Analyzes construction bid data. Its chief operating officer, Mark Zurada, stated the company sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset, settling closer to 500 today.
  • NationGraph: Serves midsize vendors, such as janitorial service providers, and claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients.

📊 Request Volume Comparison

Company Stated Request Volume
SmartProcure ~180,000 per year
Pursuit ~180,000 per year
PinPoint Analytics ~500 per day (currently)
NationGraph ~10,000 per day

#FOIA #GovTech #DataCollection #PublicRecords

Source: AI is straining America’s open records systems

item.title: Anthropic IPO Closes at $97, Largest Raise in History
item.description:
Anthropic IPO Closes at $97, Largest Raise in History

Anthropic listed on Nasdaq under the ticker $ANT, pricing its Initial Public Offering at $83 per share. The stock closed at $97.17, marking a 17% increase from the offering price before drifting to $92.60 after the close. The opening trade hit $111.50, which was 34% above the IPO price, placing the company near a $2 trillion fully diluted valuation.

💰 The Record Raise

Anthropic’s $81.3 billion offering overtook SpaceX’s June IPO to become the largest in history, beating SpaceX’s $75 billion raise. The company expected net proceeds of $104.8 billion, a figure that includes a concurrent private placement. During the IPO process, AMD agreed to invest an additional $2.5 billion in Anthropic.

📉 Market Outlook

Analysts expect lockup expiries to weigh on the stock price as approximately one trillion dollars’ worth of shares free up over the next year. This timing coincides with the company’s challenge of maintaining its position as the world’s top model provider.

📊 Financial Metrics

Metric Detail
Revenue Requirement Bear case estimates require ~$602B/yr to achieve a 20% return on ~$1T in compute commitments at a 40% operating margin and 17% tax
Comparison Required revenue exceeds Alphabet ($471B) and Apple ($478B), equating to two-thirds of the $908B earned by all 76 software/IT companies in the S&P 1500
Cash Position Anthropic raised ~$140B and still holds ~$132B on its balance sheet, implying a cash burn of under $10 billion

👥 Stakeholders and Governance

Class F shares, held by co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei, carry 50.1% of the voting power on most shareholder matters. Google owns a 13.7% stake in the company. SEC filings suggest the average employee could now be worth over $40 million, meaning the 5,300 founders and employees collectively hold more wealth than the bottom third of US households (approximately 45 million families). After-tax reality checks suggest the median employee likely takes home closer to $5 million than the headline figures.

🛡️ Safety Commitments

In their founders’ letter, Dario and Daniela Amodei committed to pacing the training and deployment of AI systems based on whether they could keep them safe and under human control. General Catalyst, an early backer, framed the company’s origin as a contrarian idea by seven people: that the safest way to build AI is also the best way. Notably, Dustin Moskovitz, an early funder, has reportedly not spoken to the co-founders in over a year and no longer speaks to Zuckerberg, Altman, or Holden Karnofsky.

🏆 Product Standing

On the day of the IPO, Anthropic was the #1 lab on Code Arena WebDev, with its model Claude Fable 5.2 scoring 1824, which is 27 points higher than the next lab.

#Anthropic #IPO #AI #Nasdaq #AMZ #TechFinance

Source: Anthropic successfully completes largest IPO in history, valued at $1.5T — Latent Space

item.title: Perplexity hits $1B revenue; Qwen4-Max and OpenAI evals released
item.description:
Perplexity hits $1B revenue; Qwen4-Max and OpenAI evals released

Perplexity has crossed a $1B annual revenue run rate, according to CEO Aravind Srinivas, while Alibaba’s Qwen4-Max preview moved to a shipping model and OpenAI granted external partners access to its internal systems for evaluation.

🔍 Overview

  • Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas told Semafor that the company crossed a $1B annual revenue run rate.
  • The Information previously reported Perplexity was under $250M at the start of the year and over $750M by August.
  • The growth was partly driven by its product, Computer.
  • At typical agent lab multiples, this revenue level suggests a valuation of roughly $30-50B for Perplexity.
  • This performance builds on a $20B funding round in September 2025.

🧩 How it works

  • Perplexity Features:
    • September’s Automations allow the system to pick up recurring tasks.
    • November’s Teammates handle ongoing jobs.
    • Computer runs fully locally on supported Macs.
    • The Monitor API watches a topic or page and triggers a webhook when relevant changes occur.
  • Qwen4-Max Specifications:
    • Total parameter count is 2.4T, with 71B active per token (a 25% reduction).
    • Accepts images and text with a 1M-token context window.
    • Smaller open-weight Qwen4 models are planned for release.
  • OpenAI Evaluation Program:
    • Apollo, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire have internal access to OpenAI models and systems.
    • Apollo places six evaluators onsite for four months.
    • METR reviews OpenAI’s largest RL run with access to transcripts, monitor records, and checkpoint snapshots.
    • Transluce conducts a six-week audit of post-training alignment evals, with a fuller follow-up in early 2027.
    • Goodfire embeds interpretability researchers to monitor training runs.

⚙️ Key details

  • Qwen4-Max Performance:

    • Scored 43 on the Intelligence Index at the highest reasoning setting, up from 34.
    • Average cost fell from $10.02 to $3.27 per task.
    • Alibaba cut output pricing from $6 to $4.50 per million tokens; the model generated about 39% fewer tokens.
    • On Arena, it ranks #14 overall and is the top Chinese model, with +7.5% net over 14.7k sessions.
    • Placed #6 in Code Arena WebDev at 1750, up 74 points from its predecessor.
    • Placed #6 in Image-to-WebDev, just above Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6 Sol.
    • Ranked #11 overall on Vals, with gains in coding and finance.
    • On HLAB, it gets 95.7% of checklist items right but passes only 21.3% of tasks, with output tokens rising 3.6x.
    • Roboflow notes it is underwhelming on its VLM benchmark compared to Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic.
    • At high reasoning effort, it is ~4.5x faster and ~68% cheaper per image than Qwen3.8-Max.

  • Competitor Benchmark:

    • Kimi K3.1 Pro cost $3.68 per index task and scored 67% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, compared to Qwen’s 48%.

💡 Why it matters

  • Perplexity’s revenue milestone qualifies it for the “>$10B fundraise” rule, marking a significant valuation increase.
  • The new Perplexity research lab has access to 10,000+ GPUs and plans to publish papers, data, models, and code.
  • OpenAI’s decision to grant internal access to independent evaluators represents a structured approach to external safety and alignment auditing.

#Perplexity #Qwen4-Max #OpenAI #AIEvaluations #Revenue

Source: Perplexity hits a $1B revenue run rate, up 4x in 2026 — Latent Space

item.title: Instinct AI Agent Secures $1 B Series C, Valued at $10 B
item.description:
Instinct AI Agent Secures $1 B Series C, Valued at $10 B

Instinct, a viral AI agent, announced a massive Series C financing round that values the company at $10 billion.

🔍 Overview

  • Series C round size: $1 billion
  • Company valuation post‑funding: $10 billion
  • The deal is expected to close by the end of the year and is valued at $8.2 billion.

💰 Funding Details

  • The round is anticipated to be Instinct’s last before its delayed public debut scheduled for 2027.
  • A $300 million employee tender was co‑led by Wellington and T. Rowe Price.
  • Flow Engineering, which is bringing the AI agent to hardware design, secured Roelof Botha as an angel investor and board member.

📅 Timeline

  • Expected closing: by year’s end.
  • Public debut: delayed to 2027, after this final private round.

📊 Why It Matters

  • The size of the financing underscores strong investor confidence in agentic AI technology.
  • The involvement of prominent investors such as Wellington, T. Rowe Price, and Roelof Botha signals broad institutional interest.
  • Positioning the round as the final pre‑IPO raise suggests Instinct is gearing up for a public market entry after a period of rapid growth.

#Instinct #AIAgents #Funding #SeriesC

item.title: a16z Launches Horowitz Andreessen Academy for Silicon Valley Startup Pipeline
item.description:
a16z Launches Horowitz Andreessen Academy for Silicon Valley Startup Pipeline

Venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) is creating the Horowitz Andreessen Academy, a pipeline designed for young people to build or join a Silicon Valley startup.

🔍 Overview

Led by a16z with $42 million in funding, the academy is described as a “highly selective school” that does not grant any accreditation or degree. It is designed mainly for recent high school graduates.

🧩 How it works

The program replaces traditional academic structures with a focus on industry experience:

  • Curriculum: Short, high-impact classes led by tech figureheads, such as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.
  • Practical Experience: “Co-ops” that provide students with roles at tech companies.
  • Assessment: There are no traditional grades, tests, or homework.

⚙️ Key details

Students in the program are provided with specific financial and technical resources:

  • More than $50,000 in compute credits
  • A $5,000 travel and research budget offered by a16z
Partner Role

🚀 Availability

  • Launch Date: The first one-year program begins in the fall of 2027.
  • Cost: The first program will be free.
  • Capacity: Only 50 students will be accepted.
  • Requirements: Students must move to San Francisco and arrange their own housing.

💡 Why it matters

The academy follows a trend of Silicon Valley billionaires, including Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, and Jeff Bezos, investing in their own schools. a16z founders Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz have been critical of colleges; Andreessen reportedly called the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Stanford “political lobbying operations fighting American innovation” in a group chat with tech leaders and White House officials.

#a16z #SiliconValley #Education #Startups

Source: Andreessen Horowitz is launching an ‘academy’ with no homework and partnerships with Palantir, Google, and Meta
